title: Falafel
subtitle: Deep-fried chickpea falafel: crisp outside, tender and herb-flecked inside
excerpt: Real falafel is made from dried chickpeas soaked overnight, never tinned. Tinned chickpeas are too wet and will produce a dense, mushy result that falls apart in the oil. Plan 12 hours ahead.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from classic Lebanese falafel technique documentation.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze shaped, uncooked falafel on a tray until solid, then transfer to a bag. Fry from frozen, adding 2 minutes to the cooking time.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch easily; the processor handles larger volumes well. Fry in batches as usual.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The shaped falafel mixture keeps refrigerated for up to 24 hours before frying.
recipe.temperatureNote: Oil for frying should reach 175 C. Use a probe thermometer to check.

content.text: This recipe uses dried chickpeas soaked overnight (NOT tinned; see the ingredient note). Tinned chickpeas contain too much moisture for the mixture to hold together during frying and will produce a dense, falling-apart result. Plan ahead: the dried chickpeas need at least 12 hours soaking. Do not be tempted to cook them; soaked-but-raw chickpeas are what gives falafel its characteristic grainy, light interior.

items.prepNote: dried chickpeas soaked overnight (NOT tinned; see recipe notes). Tinned chickpeas will not work for falafel as they are too wet.

content.text: Soak the chickpeas. Place the dried chickpeas in a large bowl and cover generously with cold water: they will roughly double in size. Leave for at least 12 hours (overnight). Drain and rinse thoroughly before use.

Process the mixture. Add the drained soaked chickpeas to the food processor with the onion, garlic, coriander, parsley, cumin, coriander-ground, chilli flakes and 1 teaspoon of salt. Pulse, scraping the sides frequently, until the mixture resembles rough breadcrumbs: it should hold together when pressed but not be smooth or paste-like. Do not over-process or the falafel will be dense. Add the baking powder and sesame oil and pulse twice to combine.

Test the mixture. Take a small amount, squeeze it firmly in your hand: it should hold its shape cleanly. If it crumbles apart, pulse briefly again. If it seems too wet, add a tablespoon of plain flour and pulse to combine. Refrigerate the mixture for 30 minutes: this firms it up and makes shaping easier.

Shape the falafel. Scoop tablespoon-sized portions and roll firmly between your palms into balls or slightly flattened discs. Place on a tray lined with baking paper. This recipe makes approximately 20 falafel.

Heat the oil. Pour the sunflower oil into a large saucepan to a depth of about 8 cm. Heat over medium-high heat to 175 C. Use a probe thermometer to verify the temperature: too cool and the falafel absorb oil and are greasy; too hot and the outside burns before the inside cooks through.

Fry in batches. Carefully lower 4 to 5 falafel into the hot oil at a time: do not crowd the pan. Fry for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden brown all over. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper. Allow the oil to return to 175 C between batches.

Serve immediately. Falafel are best eaten within 15 minutes of frying. Serve in flatbread with hummus, pickled vegetables, sliced cucumber and tomato, and a drizzle of tahini thinned with a little lemon juice and water.

items.symptom: Falafel fall apart in the oil
items.cause: Tinned chickpeas were used instead of soaked dried chickpeas, or the mixture was over-processed to a paste.
items.fix: This recipe requires soaked dried chickpeas: there is no substitute. If the mixture is already made and too wet, chill it for 1 hour and try adding a tablespoon of plain flour to bind. Test one falafel in the oil before frying the whole batch.

items.cause: The frying oil was not hot enough when the falafel went in.
items.fix: The oil must be at 175 C before each batch. Let it recover fully between batches. A thermometer is not optional here.

items.symptom: Outside is dark but inside is raw-tasting
items.cause: The oil was too hot, cooking the outside too quickly.
items.fix: Reduce the oil temperature to 170 C and fry for a longer time. Falafel are ready when they feel firm rather than soft when pressed gently.

items.cause: Under-seasoned mixture, or the spices were old and had lost potency.
items.fix: Fry a small test falafel, taste and adjust the raw mixture with more salt, cumin and chilli flakes before shaping the rest.
